transcription.text: Hi, just a quick second channel video. This is just a quick test in response to an issue on the EEVblog forum about the 121GW that Keane, here in Sydney, I think you've seen him on one of my blogs before.
Anyway, he's got a 121GW which basically blew up between a couple of the tracks on the range switches, and we don't really know how it actually happened.
And I'm still investigating this. Could be some freak thing. It could be like an issue with his particular meter. We're not entirely sure.

So we've ruled out a few things, but just one thing I wanted to test which has been, which is one of the considerations, is a high voltage DC load instead of like an impulse transient like you do in the UL testing, you know, the 8kV transient testing and all that.

I thought we'd try a DC voltage here, and I know this is going to work because I've tried it before. So we've got the range switch in the volts position like this, which I believe is the position that it died for Keane's unit.
And of course there is a PTC, a nominal 1.5k PTC, and a 1k high voltage protection resistor as well in series, and then it's clamped via two 575V MOVs in there.

So I thought we'd just actually wind the wick up on my high voltage power supply here. We'll just take it up, and just see that it survives the maximum that this power supply is capable of, which is 1200V.

So let's go up, it's going to beep at over 600V, that's a feature of the meter, it displays the warning indicator on there, a little lightning bolt. This one goes up to 11V of course, so let's turn it up to 11V, and that's now 1210V.

There you go. And you can see that on my triplet analog meter over here, it's got a 6000V DC range there. So unfortunately that's the highest I can go up to in the lab. I do have another one of these, but they're actually mains earth reference, so I can't stack them in series unfortunately.

But there you go, it survives 1200V DC, no problems whatsoever. Obviously that's just not enough to kick the MOVs into action. If it was, then we'd see the overload current limit come on here. But it can continually sustain that 1200V DC, not a problem at all.

So there you go, I just wanted to show that we're still investigating this, and if we come to any conclusion, we'll let you know. But at this stage, yeah, we're just not sure. I have to get Keen's unit back, but I suspect it's not going to tell us much. Probably my leading theory at the moment is that... let's just not have that beep anymore, shall we?

Oh, there we go. There we go. Jeez. That's because these ones are over there. Why can't these go to 11 as well? They only go to 10. What a bummer. Only this one goes to 11. Anyway, still goes to 11. I like it.

Anyway, my leading theory at the moment is potentially that Keen's meter actually had possibly some form of contaminant or contamination on the, you know, some sort of thing on or under the range switch in there that potentially might have caused it to arc over and then start that issue.

But the problem with that is, is that it's a... it'd have to be like a freaky circumstance where he actually applied well over a thousand volts to it and at a voltage before the MOVs kicked over and then, like, was arcing... well, no, it may not have been that high if it had some sort of contaminant in there. Maybe it could have arced over at a lower voltage or something like that and sustained the arc.

But then he would have had to have applied a continuous high voltage, high current capable or reasonable, you know, at least a reasonable power capability DC supply to the thing. If it's just like an impulse, like a surge or something like that, the MOVs should kick in. That's the, you know, that's the whole idea and the reason why this thing is UL tested to survive those pulses and everything else.

But I believe Keaton doesn't know on exactly, because it's not like a puff of smoke escaped. I think he only noticed the problem later when it was, like, he was using it and it was, like, out of spec. It started reading funny. I don't think he actually noticed the exact point and under the exact circumstances that it actually blew up.

So, yeah, we just, I, it's just one of those things. We don't know. Anyway, that's probably my leading theory at the moment is that we had an individual unit that's contaminated under strange driving circumstances. Because he said he was, like, driving, he was, like, measuring a DC to DC converter over a long line or something like that. What, the long line? You know, the inductance and capacitive of the long line? But, like, it's just like a low voltage DC to DC converter.
So, anyway, it's a very puzzling sort of failure mode. But I just wanted to show you that it survives that 1200 volts. No wuckers. Catch you next time.
